The long-string instrument is an experimental chordophone: extremely long strings put the fundamental below the roughly twenty hertz the ear can hear, producing beating and the higher natural overtones; the attack travels along the string as a longitudinal wave, making a sound like a science-fiction laser gun or the power cables above a train. The version by the American composer Ellen Fullman has strings about twenty-seven metres long, tensioned with C-clamps, with resonators at the ends, and the player walks along the strings rubbing them with rosin-coated hands. Such instruments have also been used for recordings, performances and sound installations by Alvin Lucier, Terry Fox, Jon Rose, Paul Panhuysen, George Smits, Yuri Landman and Sonoscopia in Porto, Portugal.
長弦樂器曾由梅森用於測試伽利略假設，使弦振動速度可見可數；0.33公尺弦發440: The long-string instrument was used by Mersenne to test Galileo's hypothesis, making the speed of a string's vibration visible and countable; a string 0.33 m long sounds 440 Hz, and a string 2.64 m long — eight times as long at the same mass and tension — sounds 55 Hz. In 1977 Alvin Lucier composed for a single-string instrument up to 25 metres long; in 1981 Terry Fox recorded two pieces; from 1983 Jon Rose bowed fences around the world. Ellen Fullman invented a long-string instrument about 27 metres long, tuned in just intonation, with the player walking along the strings and rubbing them with rosin-coated hands. Panhuysen, Smits, Landman and the Porto sound-research centre also developed large installations, polystyrene amplification, portable electric and permanent electric versions.
長弦樂器的基頻常低於人耳可聽範圍，發聲不依賴可聽基頻，而以拍頻與較高自然泛音為主: A long-string instrument's fundamental is often below the audible range, so the sound does not depend on an audible fundamental but on beating and the higher natural overtones; the string length gives a reverberation as short as about five to ten metres, or a longer echo beyond ten metres. The attack travels along the string as a longitudinal wave, producing a sound like a laser gun or the power cables above a train. Fullman's version is centred on the octave of middle C and extends an octave above and below, and the strings of the lower octave can run the full length. Volume and resonance are decided by the tension of the C-clamps, the friction of the rosin-coated hands, the resonators at the ends, and the electrical or polystyrene amplification.
